title: Notification System
oneLine: Accept notification intent once, resolve preferences and templates, enqueue by channel, deliver through provider adapters, and track retries, dedupe, and status independently.
opening: I would model a notification as durable intent rather than a direct provider call. A producer sends an idempotent request containing event, recipient, template, variables, priority, and schedule. The notification service validates it, resolves user preferences and quiet hours, renders a versioned template, persists the notification, and publishes channel-specific jobs. Independent email, SMS, push, and in-app workers apply rate limits and provider routing, then record delivery attempts and status events. Retries use exponential backoff and a DLQ; provider callbacks update delivered/bounced/opened states asynchronously. Critical transactional notifications and bulk marketing traffic use separate queues and capacity so a campaign cannot delay OTPs or trade alerts.
ask: Which channels and delivery guarantees are required?
Transactional, marketing, or both—and what priorities/SLOs?
Do users have preferences, quiet hours, locale, or fallback channels?
Is the requirement accepted, sent, delivered, or exactly one visible notification?
scale: Estimate notifications by channel because provider throughput and payload sizes differ.
Separate burst ingestion capacity from provider send rate; queues absorb the mismatch.
Store attempt history with retention tiers—hot operational status versus long-term audit/analytics.

decisions.why: Provider calls and callbacks cannot generally participate in one transaction.
decisions.switch: Use stronger transactional boundaries only inside your system, then keep external effects idempotent.

decisions.default: Separate channels and priority classes; isolate transactional from bulk.
decisions.why: Different providers, retry behavior, and SLOs otherwise create head-of-line blocking.
decisions.switch: Tenant-dedicated queues for regulated or very large customers.

decisions.default: Versioned templates rendered before provider send, with locale and schema validation.
decisions.why: Retries should reproduce the intended message and not silently use a newer template.
decisions.switch: Provider-side templates may reduce payload/cost but create version drift and lock-in.

decisions.default: Health/cost/region-aware adapter with circuit breakers and fallback.
decisions.why: No single external provider should be a platform SPOF.
decisions.switch: Do not fail over blindly if sender identity, regulatory consent, or message semantics differ.

deepDives.title: Idempotency and dedupe
points: Producer supplies an idempotency key scoped to event and recipient.
Persist accepted intent and publish with a transactional outbox.
Workers record provider request ID and suppress repeat side effects where possible.

deepDives.title: Status model
points: Distinguish accepted, queued, attempted, provider-accepted, delivered, failed, bounced, and opened.
Callbacks may arrive late, duplicated, or out of order; apply monotonic/state-machine rules.
Expose honest semantics—provider accepted is not user delivered.

deepDives.title: Compliance
points: Honor consent, unsubscribe, quiet hours, data locality, and retention.
Redact sensitive template variables from logs.
Audit policy and template version used for every send.

failures.response: End-to-end idempotency key, outbox, worker dedupe, and provider request IDs; accept that some channels still need reconciliation.
Circuit breaker, bounded retries, alternative provider, queue age alert, and explicit degraded-channel policy.
Separate priority queues, worker pools, quotas, and reserved provider capacity.
Schema validation, retry classification, DLQ with safe replay tooling, and template canarying.

questions.q: How do you guarantee an OTP is sent only once?
questions.a: Guarantee one accepted notification intent and use idempotency through the provider call, but external uncertainty means you may still retry. Make OTP consumption single-use so duplicate delivery cannot duplicate the protected action.
Store schedule time durably, move near-due items into queues via time buckets or a delayed queue, and make the handoff idempotent. Re-evaluate preferences at send time if policy requires it.

questions.q: What if a callback arrives before the send response?
questions.a: Persist events with provider IDs and apply a state machine that accepts out-of-order evidence. Do not assume transport order between API response and webhook.

Track accepted-to-provider and accepted-to-delivered latency by channel/priority, queue age, retry rate, bounce/error taxonomy, provider availability, and user-visible success—not only worker throughput.

mistakes: Calling providers directly from product services
seniorSignal: Separate intent, policy, delivery, and evidence. Discuss priority isolation, provider uncertainty, compliance, transactional outbox, and truthful status semantics.
implementation: Provider adapters behind Resilience4j circuit breakers
Redis token buckets; webhook handlers with monotonic status transitions
